\chapter{El donativo}
\label{ch:es-donar}
\hlchaptermodality{461}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read a collection appeal: what may be donated, what will be turned away and why, and where to hand it in.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[donar]{donar — to give it away}

\label{lesson:ES-C461-donar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{perdón} and \textbf{la sangre}. There is a verb of giving hiding in the first, and the second is the commonest thing it is used about.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: donar}
\textbf{donar} — to donate.

\emph{Donar sangre} — to give blood, the sign outside every mobile clinic. \emph{Donar ropa} — to donate clothes. \textbf{La donación} is the donation and \textbf{el donante} the donor.

It is not the everyday verb for giving. \emph{Dar} is that. \emph{Donar} is giving to an institution or a cause, and it carries no expectation of return.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: donar is not regalar}]
Three verbs of giving, and the difference is who receives:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what is happening} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
handing anything to anyone & \textbf{dar} \\
making somebody a present & \textbf{regalar} \\
giving to a cause or a body & \textbf{donar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Te doy el taladro} — I'm passing it to you. \emph{Te regalo el taladro} — it is yours, a gift. \emph{Dono el taladro al centro} — the neighbourhood centre has it now.

Use \emph{donar} about a person and it sounds like a charitable act rather than a kindness, which is sometimes exactly the joke a Spanish speaker is making.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{donare}, to give — and here is the payoff on a word you have had since the courtesy chapter, long before you could take it apart.

\textbf{Perdón} is \emph{per-} plus \emph{donare}: to \textbf{give thoroughly}, to give completely away. Forgiving somebody is giving the offence away rather than holding it, and the metaphor is the same in English — \emph{for-give} is built the identical way, \emph{for-} being an intensifier, so \emph{pardon} and \emph{forgive} are the same idea twice.

The family also gives \emph{el don}, a gift or a talent. And off to one side sits \textbf{la dosis} — not from \emph{donare} but from Greek's own word for a giving, off the same ancient root: a dose is what is \emph{given} to you.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to give blood
  \item I'm donating the tools to the centre
  \item what \emph{perdón} is made of
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To donate? (\textbf{Donar}.) The donor? (\textbf{El donante}.) What does \emph{perdón} literally say? (\textbf{To give thoroughly} — to give it away.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[peligroso]{peligroso — dangerous}

\label{lesson:ES-C461-peligroso}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el taladro} and \textbf{el accidente}. One can lead to the other, and the sign warning you sits between them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: peligroso}
\textbf{peligroso} — dangerous.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Peligro.} No pasar.
\end{quote}

\textbf{El peligro} is the noun and the single word on the sign; \textbf{peligroso} is the adjective. \emph{Una zona peligrosa} — a dangerous area. \emph{Es peligroso dejarlo ahí} — it's dangerous to leave it there.

\emph{Estar en peligro} is to be in danger, and \emph{fuera de peligro} — out of danger — uses the frame you already have from \emph{fuera de servicio}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -oso makes an adjective of a noun}]
\textbf{-oso} means \textquotedblleft{}full of\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}given to\textquotedblright{}, and it turns nouns into adjectives all over the language:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{adjective} \\
\midrule
el peligro & peligr\textbf{oso} \\
el cuidado & cuidad\textbf{oso} — careful \\
la fama & fam\textbf{oso} — famous \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English has the same ending in \emph{dangerous}, \emph{famous} and \emph{curious}, from the same Latin \emph{-osus}, so the pair usually translates straight across.

It agrees like any adjective — \emph{peligrosa}, \emph{peligrosos} — and the noun keeps its own gender: \emph{el peligro} is masculine, \emph{una zona peligrosa} feminine.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{periculum}, a trial or a risk — from a root meaning \textbf{to try}, the one also behind \emph{experiri}, to test by going through.

So a \emph{peligro} is something you have to \textbf{try your luck against}, and English \textbf{peril} is the same word, kept closer to the Latin. \textbf{Experience} and \textbf{experiment} are relatives too: all of them are attempts, and only some are survived.

From \emph{periculum} to \emph{peligro} the \textbf{r} and the \textbf{l} swapped places — the metathesis you met in \emph{milagro} from \emph{miraculum}. Both words came through speech, and both got their letters shuffled on the way; a word that arrived by book was never shuffled: \textbf{periclitar}, to be in danger, keeps \emph{periculum}'s letters in their Latin order, and stands beside the spoken \emph{peligro} as the same word at two speeds.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item danger, do not enter
  \item the drill is dangerous for a child
  \item which other word swapped its r and l the same way
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Dangerous? (\textbf{Peligroso}.) The noun? (\textbf{El peligro}.) What did \emph{periculum} mean? (\textbf{A trial, a risk} — something you try your luck against.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rechazar]{rechazar — to turn it down}

\label{lesson:ES-C461-rechazar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{aceptar} and \textbf{admitir}. The word coming next undoes the first, and it is made of the same Latin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: rechazar}
\textbf{rechazar} — to turn down, to reject, to refuse.

\emph{Rechazar una oferta} — to turn down an offer. \emph{Han rechazado la solicitud} — the application has been rejected. \emph{El banco rechazó la tarjeta} — the card was declined.

\textbf{El rechazo} is the noun: a refusal, and in medicine the rejection of a transplant.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three verbs of the counter, completed}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the move} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
you agree to what is offered & \textbf{aceptar} \\
the institution lets it through & \textbf{admitir} \\
it is turned back & \textbf{rechazar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Rechazar} is the mirror of \textbf{both} of the others, and which one it mirrors depends on who is doing it. A shop \emph{rechaza} your card where it might have \emph{aceptado} it; an office \emph{rechaza} your form where it might have \emph{admitido} it.

Notices usually phrase a refusal by negating the other two — \emph{no se aceptan}, \emph{no se admiten} — but \emph{rechazar} takes the same \emph{se} form when the refusing itself is the point: \emph{se rechazan los rotos}. In the plain active it is a person who does it: \emph{rechacé la oferta}.

Note the spelling: \textbf{rechacé}, with a \textbf{c}. Spanish spelling prefers \textbf{c} before \emph{e}, so a stem \emph{z} turns into a \emph{c} right through the conjugation, which is why \emph{empezar} gives \emph{empecé}. A handful of borrowings keep the \emph{z} — \emph{zen}, \emph{zeta} — but no verb ending does.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{re-} plus \emph{chazar}, to drive back — a verb Spanish took from Old French \emph{chacier}, and behind that Vulgar Latin \textbf{captiare}, to chase, built on \textbf{capere}, \textbf{to take}. That French leg is why this word has \textbf{ch}: Spanish's own inherited form of \emph{captiare} is \textbf{cazar}, to hunt.

So \emph{rechazar} and \textbf{aceptar} are cousins, and the pair is worth holding: \emph{ad-} plus \emph{capere} is taking a thing \textbf{towards} you, and \emph{re-} plus \emph{captiare} is driving it \textbf{back}. One Latin verb of taking, pointed two ways by two prefixes.

The same \emph{captiare} gave Spanish \textbf{cazar}, to hunt, and French \emph{chasser}, which English borrowed as \textbf{chase} — and, through a second borrowing, as \textbf{catch}. To reject something is to chase it back the way it came.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item they have rejected the application
  \item I turned the offer down, in the past
  \item what \emph{rechazar} and \emph{aceptar} have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To turn down? (\textbf{Rechazar}.) I turned down? (\textbf{Rechacé} — z becomes c before e.) Which verb is its cousin? (\textbf{Aceptar} — both from \emph{capere}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(donar, peligroso, rechazar)]{(donar, peligroso, rechazar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R461-repaso-donar}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all three: \emph{to donate}, \emph{dangerous}, \emph{to turn down}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one verb of taking, pointed two ways}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the prefix, and where it points} \\
\midrule
\textbf{aceptar} & \emph{ad-}, \textbf{towards} you — you take it \\
\textbf{rechazar} & \emph{re-}, \textbf{back} — you drive it away \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both are Latin \emph{capere}, to take. The prefix does everything, exactly as it did for \emph{meter}, \emph{el permiso}, \emph{permitir} and \emph{admitir} off \emph{mittere}.

That is now two families in four chapters where the prefix carries the whole meaning. When a Spanish verb starts with \emph{a-}, \emph{re-}, \emph{per-}, \emph{ad-} or \emph{des-}, the part after it is usually a word you can already find.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two words hiding in your earliest vocabulary}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{new word} & \textbf{where it was already} \\
\midrule
\textbf{donar} & \emph{perdón} — \emph{per-donare}, to give thoroughly \\
\textbf{peligroso} & \emph{el peligro}, and \emph{periculum} behind it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Perdón} is the one to keep. You learned it in the courtesy chapter as a thing you say when you bump into somebody, and it turns out to be built on \textbf{giving} — forgiveness is handing the offence over rather than keeping it. English does the identical thing in \emph{for-give}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item they turned down the application
  \item giving blood is not dangerous
  \item which everyday word has \emph{donar} inside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All three again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence about something offered and refused.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(la campaña de donación) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C461-sintesis-donar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{donar} and \textbf{rechazar}. The notice below does the first and warns about the second.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A poster in a stairwell. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{RECOGIDA DE JUGUETES}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Puede \textbf{donar} juguetes en buen estado hasta el día 30.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Se \textbf{rechazan} los que estén rotos o sean \textbf{peligrosos} para menores de tres años.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Entréguelos en portería. Gracias por colaborar.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what is being collected, and until when
  \item the two reasons something would be turned away
  \item where to hand things in
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Se rechazan los que estén rotos o sean peligrosos} is the sentence to take apart, and the subjunctive is back, doing a cousin of the job it did on the swimming-course notice. There it withheld agreement that places remained; here it withholds any claim about which toys will actually turn up.

\emph{Los que \textbf{estén} rotos}, not \emph{están}. The poster is not saying that some of the toys are broken; it is describing a \textbf{category that may or may not turn up} — whichever ones happen to be broken. The indicative would point at particular toys the writer had in mind, which on a poster addressed to a whole building would be an odd thing to imply.

Note \textbf{sean} as well: \emph{ser} for a lasting property, because a toy that is dangerous for a toddler is dangerous by design, not by circumstance. And \emph{estén} for \emph{rotos}, because being broken is a state a thing arrived at. One sentence, both verbs, each right for its own reason.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines for a collection poster: say what can be donated and until when, say what will be turned away and why, and say where to hand it in.

Then check yourself: did you use the subjunctive for the things that might turn up, and \emph{ser} against \emph{estar} for the two reasons?
\end{tcolorbox}
